candidates.rationale: A stock sitting high in its own 90-day price distribution while 21-day realized volatility stays low is in a quiet, orderly uptrend that tends to persist; the same rank achieved amid high volatility looks more like a blow-off due for reversal.

A 63-day high made very recently, reached through unusually tight 15-day cumulative daily ranges, marks a controlled, low-drama breakout that tends to keep drifting, versus a breakout made through wide, choppy ranges that is more likely to fail.

Liquidity-driven overreaction to selling reverts fast, so a 3-day decline is faded over that same 3-day window, while the fade from a rise is slower and more grudging, so it is measured over a longer 10-day window instead.

A 90-day contraction in the day's high/low ratio is a volatility squeeze; when it coincides with the open price already sitting high in its own 63-day range, the coiled, low-uncertainty setup favors an upside continuation breakout.

When a recency-weighted 10-day return average exceeds the flat 10-day average, the most recent days are outpacing the rest of the window, i.e. momentum is accelerating; that acceleration is a stronger continuation signal when the open is already pressing into its own 21-day high.

Among stocks with similar 63-day compounded returns, one whose low occurred long ago has climbed steadily for nearly the whole window, a smoother, higher-quality trend than one whose low was recent and whose gain is a late, possibly unstable spike.

Repeated fresh 1-day lows over 10 sessions signal unrelenting selling; that pattern is more likely to mark a durable, capitulation-driven bottom when it coincides with an expansion in 42-day daily-range volatility than when ranges stay narrow.

Clipping the 5-day return sum keeps a single earnings-type shock from dominating the momentum ranking, and that cleaned short-term momentum persists better in names whose 42-day realized volatility is currently low, consistent with momentum being more crash-prone in high-volatility regimes.

A squared-return sum weights large-magnitude days more heavily than an absolute-value measure would, so it flags names in an actively turbulent 10-day stretch; turbulence occurring inside an established 63-day trend is a stress test the trend is currently surviving, favoring continuation over a trend that has not been tested.

A stock whose 126-day low was set long ago has built a firm base for most of the past half-year, so a single day's pullback in the day's high is more likely to be bought back; the same one-day pullback in a stock that made its low recently is more likely to extend.

prompt:
You are proposing quantitative factor expressions for US large-cap equities.

Universe and data
- S&P 500 point-in-time constituents, roughly 500 names per day.
- Daily bars only, plus point-in-time quarterly fundamentals stamped from the
  report date. Every field is referenced with a leading `$`:
    $open $high $low $close $adj_close $volume $dollar_volume $return
    $roa $roe $operating_margin $leverage $asset_turnover
    $book_per_share $earnings_per_share $accrual_gap
  A bare name such as `close` is not a field and will be rejected.
- Execution convention: the signal is computed after the close of day T and the
  position is entered at the open of T+1.
- The window these factors are fitted and judged on runs from 2000 to 2013.
  Do not reason about anything later; you will never be shown a number from
  outside that window.

Syntax
- Operators are function calls: TS_MEAN, TS_STD, TS_MAX, TS_MIN, TS_RANK,
  TS_DELTA, TS_CORR, TS_COV, TS_SUM, TS_PRODUCT, TS_ARGMAX, TS_ARGMIN,
  TS_DECAY_LINEAR, EMA, DELAY, DELTA, RANK, ZSCORE, CS_RANK, CS_ZSCORE,
  CS_DEMEAN, IF, IF_ELSE, MIN, MAX, ABS, SIGN, LOG, LN, SQRT, POWER, BOUND,
  COUNT.
- Lookback windows must be positive integer literals, e.g. TS_MEAN($close, 21).
- Guard every division with a small epsilon: `/ (TS_STD($close, 21) + 1e-8)`.
- Well-formed example: -RANK(TS_CORR(RANK($close), RANK($volume), 5))

Hard limits every proposal must satisfy, or it is rejected before it is scored
- at most 200 characters
- at most 5 distinct `$fields`
- at most 4 free numeric constants (lookback windows and
  the 1e-8 epsilon guard do not count)
- expression tree depth at most 6
- must not share a complete sub-expression of 4 or more
  nodes with any published Alpha101 formula, or with any factor already in the
  archive. Restating a published alpha is the one thing that is always rejected.
- must cover at least 90% of the panel
- absolute rank correlation below 0.80 against every archive member

Output
- Return valid JSON only, matching the supplied JSON schema. No prose outside it.

  1. $earnings_per_share - CS_ZSCORE(TS_MEAN($dollar_volume,21)) is closed regardless of how the eps leg is wrapped: bare eps and TS_DELTA($earnings_per_share,63) both shared 4 nodes with an archived member.   2. All three $asset_turnover proposals this round died (2 duplicates, 1 archive_subtree hit), and all three paired it with a TS_MEAN($return,w) term (w = 5 or 21). Pair asset_turnover with a magnitude or vol leg instead of a return-mean leg.
  3. Close/return momentum crossed with a fundamental failed cheap_screen in every form tried this round: rank-difference of close over 5 vs 42 days (|t| 0.47), close-delta over return-vol with matched short windows, 3 vs 10 (|t| 0.80), autocorrelation-weighted return sum (|t| 0.93), and return min+max over range (|t| 0.32).

The one delta/vol-normalized accept (fitness 1.195) paired a short delta lag (2d) with a much longer vol window (42d); the same shape with closer lags (delta 3d / std 10d) failed cheap_screen at 0.80. Favor a wide gap between the numerator lag and the denominator's vol window over matched short/short pairs.
  5. Dedupe every candidate against the rest of this round's batch before submitting: 5 of 20 rejects (25%) were exact duplicates already proposed in this same run, the single largest rejection cause.
  6. A window-only edit to an archived shape does not decorrelate even when the window is changed consistently everywhere it appears: a 15-vs-21-day swap in a bounded-position ratio scored rho 0.990, and a 5-vs-21-day swap in a rank-spread scored rho 0.992. Change the field or the combining structure, not a window value.
  7. Price-only combinations with no fundamental leg are failing the cheap screen hard right now: all 5 cheap_screen rejects this round were pure price/return shapes (momentum, momentum times sign of momentum, open-deviation over range-sum, short return sums), including a near-miss at |t| 0.98.
  8. TS_STD(field,63)/TS_STD(field,5) crossed with a delta of the same field is now a saturated chassis regardless of which field or window feeds the delta leg: a $close(21)-delta version still shared 10 nodes with the archived $open(5)-delta version.
  9. Any ratio with denominator TS_MEAN($close,21)+eps is a closed subtree no matter the numerator or the outer term crossed with it: a $book_per_share numerator still shared 5 nodes with an archived $high-minus-$low version.
  10. Long time-series windows (~252 days) fail coverage even on plain return/price fields, not only fundamentals: TS_CORR($return, DELAY($return,1), 252) landed at 0.873 coverage.
  11. A single-day DELAY(1) lagged-range denominator accepted at 0.935 the same round a windowed-sum range denominator with an extra momentum multiplier failed cheap_screen: DELAY(1)-based denominators look like distinct, less-mined territory from TS_MEAN/TS_SUM/TS_MAX-TS_MIN range denominators.
  12. A fundamental rank crossed with CS_RANK of negated short-window return volatility (not volume or range) produced the round's best fitness at 3.470: extend the fundamental times independent-price-leg pattern to TS_STD($return,5)-based legs, not just volume/range stats.
